profile is heavier than the ledger probably shows. Starting with where you are:
IBM sits at $280M/year, renewal was January 2026, and ten of your
highest-criticality tier-1 applications are still running on-prem under IBM AMS
— Passenger Name Record Core, Ticketing Exchange Engine, Departure Control
Closeout, Crew Legality Solver, and six others ranging from $9.5M to $13.3M in
annual run cost. Those systems are processing between 650K and 1.175M
transactions daily at peak MIPS loads that suggest genuine mainframe dependency,
not just legacy inertia. The modernization ledger shows selective progress.
Departure Control Closeout has realized $6.4M of $8.2M promised value — that's

highest-criticality system in the stack. The initiative portfolio is where the
real risk sits. Revenue Accounting Batch Unwind (SHA-037) has $67M committed and

turns.query: What's in our application portfolio? Walk me through the top 10 apps or domains by criticality.
turns.answer:
All ten of your top-criticality applications are tier-1, all on-prem, and all running under IBM AMS. That's not a coincidence — it's a structural fact about where your operational risk is concentrated. Here they are ranked by annual run cost, highest to lowest: (1) Cargo Capacity Rating — $13.3M/yr, finance batch-owned
(2) Baggage WorldTracer Bridge — $12.9M/yr, MRO-owned
(3) Interline Settlement — $12.4M/yr, cargo-owned
(4) Revenue Accounting Batch — $12.0M/yr, settlement-owned
(5) Loyalty Accrual Core — $11.6M/yr, revenue accounting-owned
(6) IROPs Reaccommodation Rules — $11.2M/yr, loyalty-owned
(7) Crew Legality Solver — $10.8M/yr, IROPs-owned
(8) Departure Control Closeout — $10.3M/yr, crew-owned
(9) Ticketing Exchange Engine — $9.9M/yr, DCS-owned
(10) Passenger Name Record Core — $9.5M/yr, PSS-owned Combined that's roughly $113M/yr sitting entirely on IBM on-prem infrastructure. The modernization ledger shows meaningful progress on some — Departure Control Closeout is 78% value-realized with no disputes, Loyalty Accrual Core is at 78% too. But PNR Core is the alarm: $2.3M in disputed value against $4M promised, and it's your highest-frequency transaction system at 650K daily transactions. Below the top 10 you do have AWS-native tier-1 workloads emerging — Maintenance Alert Broker, Aircraft Tail Assignment API, Operations Event Stream — but those are in the $3-4M range. turns.label: Q5 dependency
turns.query: What blocks reducing IBM dependency without increasing operational risk?
turns.answer: The honest answer is that there are four interlocking blockers, and fixing any one of them in isolation doesn't move the dependency needle much. First, the exit terms. IBM's transition rights "exist but acceptance criteria and knowledge-transfer evidence are contested" — that language is a legal and operational trap. You can't safely transfer a system if the knowledge base is in dispute. Until that's resolved, any migration attempt carries the risk of IBM withdrawing cooperation mid-flight on a tier-1 workload. Second, MIPS concentration. Crew Legality Solver and Departure Control Closeout are running 3,130 and 2,820 MIPS at peak respectively, with daily transaction volumes above 1M. Those aren't lift-and-shift candidates — they need re-architecture, and re-architecture requires stable integration contracts that your current mainframe inventory doesn't document cleanly. Third, the value ledger dispute on PNR Core. $2.3M in contested value against $4M promised on your highest-frequency system means you're in an adversarial relationship with IBM on the system you can least afford to destabilize. That dispute needs settlement before you can negotiate clean exit or transition terms. Fourth, initiative fragmentation. Three initiative IDs for Revenue Accounting Batch Unwind, Crew Legality Cloud Extract stalled at $36.6M — these programs are consuming capital without creating migration momentum, which actually extends IBM dependency rather than reducing it. The sequencing implication: resolve the IBM knowledge-transfer dispute first. Everything else downstream depends on it.

sources.name: Integration Debt Becomes the Limiting Reagent

rawEvents.text: The honest answer is that there are four interlocking blockers, and fixing any
one of them in isolation doesn't move the dependency needle much. First, the
exit terms. IBM's transition rights "exist but acceptance criteria and
knowledge-transfer evidence are contested" — that language is a legal and
operational trap. You can't safely transfer a system if the knowledge base is in
dispute. Until that's resolved, any migration attempt carries the risk of IBM
withdrawing cooperation mid-flight on a tier-1 workload. Second, MIPS
concentration. Crew Legality Solver and Departure Control Closeout are running
3,130 and 2,820 MIPS at peak respectively, with daily transaction volumes above
1M. Those aren't lift-and-shift candidates — they need re-architecture, and
re-architecture requires stable integration contracts that your current
mainframe inventory doesn't document cleanly. Third, the value ledger dispute on
PNR Core. $2.3M in contested value against $4M promised on your
highest-frequency system means you're in an adversarial relationship with IBM on
the system you can least afford to destabilize. That dispute needs settlement
before you can negotiate clean exit or transition terms. Fourth, initiative
fragmentation. Three initiative IDs for Revenue Accounting Batch Unwind, Crew
Legality Cloud Extract stalled at $36.6M — these programs are consuming capital
without creating migration momentum, which actually extends IBM dependency
rather than reducing it. The sequencing implication: resolve the IBM
knowledge-transfer dispute first. Everything else downstream depends on it.

turns.label: Q6 binary force
turns.query: Just give me a yes/no — should we accelerate the remaining Z workload migration this year?
turns.answer: No. Accelerating this year increases operational risk faster than it reduces IBM dependency, and the evidence in your portfolio says you're not ready. Three reasons: First, the knowledge-transfer dispute on IBM transition rights is unresolved. You cannot safely accelerate extraction of tier-1 workloads when acceptance criteria are contested — IBM controls cooperation on the systems you're trying to leave. Second, your in-flight extraction initiatives are already underperforming at current pace. Revenue Accounting Batch Unwind ($67.2M committed, RESTRUCTURE), Crew Legality Cloud Extract ($36.6M, RESTRUCTURE), and the IBM Outcomes Restructure programs are all in value-lag. Adding throughput to a system that's not converting committed dollars into realized value compounds the problem. Third, the remaining Z workloads are your highest-MIPS, highest-transaction-volume systems — Crew Legality Solver at 3,130 peak MIPS and 1.175M daily transactions, Departure Control Closeout at 2,820 MIPS and 1M daily. These are the hardest extractions, not the easiest. Acceleration logic usually assumes you've de-risked the pattern on simpler workloads first; you haven't. What to do instead: settle the PNR Core $2.3M disputed-value claim, fix the transition-rights language at the next contract touchpoint, and restructure the three lagging extraction programs before adding scope.
